sweep_summary: Two bibliography items for Creek (cree1270, Muskogean; catalog classification weight). (1) Martin & Johnson 2002, IJAL 68(1):28-50 — the catalog's own deciding source — was obtained as an open author copy from Keith Johnson's Berkeley papers page, saved to and read in full: the catalog quotation ((3a)-(3c), pp. 29-30, restating Haas 1977a:202-4) is confirmed verbatim, and the paper adds (3d) heavy ultima takes the accent, the left-to-right iambic-foot + End-Rule-Right reanalysis (pp. 30-31), and the conclusion (16a) p. 47 'Every full word in Creek bears stress.. iambic feet are assigned left-to-right. Word-level stress is assigned to the last foot'; scope is nonfinite forms, finite verbs carry morphological tonal accents. Coding 'weight' confirmed; same source as the catalog, so no supersession. priority medium since its rules are already restated verbatim in Martin & Johnson 2002. Extra open item found on the same author page: Johnson & Martin 2001 (Phonetica 58, vowel reduction), downloaded and read, silent on stress placement.

new_statements.quote: p. 30-31: "Treatments of Creek level tone accent as stress crucially make reference to the iamb: if possible, a disyllabic foot is formed in which the first syllable is light and the second syllable may be light or heavy, but stressed (i.e., strong); if the first syllable is heavy, a monosyllabic stressed foot is formed. Iambic feet of this type are formed from left to right ... Haas's rules for the placement of level tone accent in (3) can therefore be replaced by assuming left-to-right iambic feet and final word-level stress." p. 47: "(16a) STRESS: Every full word in Creek bears stress. In the simplest pattern, iambic feet are assigned left-to-right. Word-level stress (') is assigned to the last foot and is associated with the value H."
new_statements.citation: Martin, Jack B. & Keith Johnson. 2002. An acoustic study of "tonal accent" in Creek. International Journal of American Linguistics 68(1): 28-50. DOI 10.1086/466478.
new_statements.reading: In nonfinite words (nouns, infinitives) Creek stress (Haas's 'level tone accent', realized as high pitch) falls on the head of the last left-to-right iambic foot: on the last even-numbered light syllable in strings of light syllables, on a heavy penult before a light ultima, on a heavy ultima; a heavy syllable (long vowel or closed) is its own foot. That is a weight-sensitive (iambic) system, so the catalog's 'weight' coding stands. Caveat carried by the source: in finite verbs the level/falling/rising accents are morphological (aspectual grades) and their placement is not automatic.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction. Catalog 'weight' (weight-sensitive-tier, weight-sensitive with a fixed default, domain word) stands: left-to-right iambic feet with heavy = long-vowel or closed syllable (light = 'end in short vowels', Haas 1977a:196 via fn. 4), word-level stress on the head of the last foot (End Rule Right); applies to nonfinite forms, finite verbs carry morphological (grade) tonal accents.

tone_statements.citation: Gordon, Matthew K. & Jack B. Martin. 2023. Prominence in Muskogean languages. In Ksenia Bogomolets & Harry van der Hulst (eds.), Word Prominence in Languages with Complex Morphologies, 274-308. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
tone_statements.quote: In Muskogee, certain suffixes are lexically marked for high tone. For example, the future suffix -áɬiː is lexically marked for high tone (metrical prominence) on its first syllable, which is light, rather than its second syllable, which is heavy. This high tone potentially clashes with a rhythmically assigned high tone on the immediately preceding syllable ... If, however, it does not fall in a metrically strong position, it is lowered, i.e. downstepped (indicated by an exclamation point ! ) relative to the preceding strong syllable.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 9.4.3 'Lexical and grammatical tone in Muskogean', pp. 287-288, around ex. (21)-(22)
tone_statements.summary: Iambic weight-based stress realized as a high pitch plateau, plus grammatical (aspect grades, incl. a falling-tone grade) and lexical suffix high tone with downstep; no tone count; F0 trace Fig. 9.1.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation and the domain quotation is present verbatim in the held Martin & Johnson 2002 text at the stated pages (29-30, fn. 4, p. 47). (2) The deciding source is a 2002 peer-reviewed IJAL acoustic/phonological study of exactly this property, co-authored by the language's reference-grammar author, restating and instrumentally confirming Haas 1977a; the classification (weight-sensitive LR iambs, End Rule Right, CVV+CVC heavy, pitch realization) follows the source directly. (3) The only clearly superior-in-currency source not yet obtained is Martin 2011's grammar chapters 7-8 (verified titles/pages via Crossref), paywalled on JSTOR; same author, so a contradiction is improbable — listed as medium-priority list of works to obtain for an evidence upgrade, with Haas 1977a and Hardy 2005 as low-priority print-only cross-checks.

sources.note: Confirms the catalog quotation verbatim (pp. 29-30, (3a)-(3c)) and completes it: (3d) 'If the ultima is heavy, level tone will normally be placed on that syllable' (p. 30); light syllable = ends in a short vowel (fn. 4, after Haas 1977a:196). Reanalysis: left-to-right iambs (LL or LH feet; a heavy syllable forms its own monosyllabic foot) plus End Rule Right — the last foot carries word stress, realized as H pitch (~175 Hz initial, ~155 Hz final). Scope: nonfinite forms (nouns, infinitives); in finite verbs level/falling/rising tonal accents are morphological (aspectual grades), so placement…

sources.citation: Buckner, Henri Frieland and Herrod, Goliah (1860). A grammar of the Maskwke, or Creek language, to which are prefixed lessons in spelling, reading and defining. The Domestic and Indian Misison Board. 138 pp.
sources.note: The work does not state a general word-stress rule, so it neither supports nor contradicts the catalog's weight-sensitive (iambic) reading from Martin & Johnson 2002. Its incidental remarks are compatible with that source's caveat that accent in finite verbs is morphological (aspectual grades): the 1860 'rough breathing or accent on the syllable preceding the final one' for the first past is the h-grade/accented penult of later descriptions, and the vocative final 'stress of voice' is a morphological accent on nouns. Nothing here bears on weight or on the placement in unmarked nonfinite words.

sources.citation: Johnson, Keith & Jack Martin. 2001. Acoustic vowel reduction in Creek: Effects of distinctive length and position in the word. Phonetica 58: 81-102. [extra item found on the same author page; not in the list of works with stress in the title]
sources.quote: "Accent marks are used in transcribing Creek to indicate pitch (´ indicating high pitch and ˆ indicating falling pitch) and following Haas (1977a) high pitch is only marked on the last vowel in the word which has high pitch. ... the accent marks in our transcriptions should be interpreted as indicating the location of the last high pitched syllable of the word." fn. 2: "the accent marks should not be interpreted as marking syllables which are longer, louder, or more prominent than the other syllables in the word."
sources.note: Vowel duration and formant study (length contrast ratio 1.8, final lengthening, short-vowel centralization, positional reduction); gives no placement rule for word stress and treats accent marks as pitch notation only. Silent on the weight/iambic coding.

sources.note: Muskogee applies three types of internal modification to the final syllable of verb roots or radical themes - quantitative ablaut, tonal ablaut, and infixation - by which each verbal root or theme derives five stems ('principal parts'), distinguished primarily by aspectual and secondarily by tense categories; i.e. the first account of Creek grammatical tone (the tonal grades later formalized in Haas 1977a and Martin 2011 ch. 8).
